## [From CSR Claims to Legitimacy Gaps: Abductive Topic Modeling of Fashion Communication Across the Fashion Supply Chain](../publications/9dc102fa87b4b7f04354.md)

Hye Seung Jeong; Yoo‐Kyoung Seock

ABSTRACT Fiber‐Textile‐Apparel‐Retail \(FTAR\) firms communicate their fashion corporate social responsibility \(fCSR\) efforts to stakeholders to obtain operational legitimacy\. However, little is known about the extent to which fCSR disclosures align with stakeholder expectations and sustainability principles\. To address this gap, this study integrates legitimacy and stakeholder theories, legitimacy gaps, and the Triple Bottom Line‐Sustainable Development Goals \(TBL‐SDG\) framework\. fCSR disclosures from 297 webpages of 80 FTAR firms were analyzed and interpreted using an abductive topic modeling approach\. The results yielded three topics and six subtopics, revealing an underrepresentation of environmental sustainability\. Legitimacy gaps were also identified between conformance claims and outcome evidence, stakeholder recognition and participation, and information disclosure and its evidence of usefulness, indicating that communicated fCSR remained insufficiently substantiated across legitimacy dimensions\. FTAR firms can address these gaps by complementing standards, targets, and governance disclosures with verified outcomes, meaningful stakeholder participation, and evidence that disclosures provide practical benefits\.

## [Device\-level stochastic switching enables tunable short\-term memory in magnetic tunnel junction neurons](../publications/9dcff8c9930157f7427e.md)

Jingli Liu; Huannan Zheng; Zhaoyu Hao; Yuanzhuo Ji; Kezhou Yang

Short\-term memory is essential for temporal information processing, yet its hardware implementation commonly requires recurrent connections or additional state storage\. Here, we demonstrate a device\-level short\-term memory mechanism enabled by stochastic switching in magnetic tunnel junction neurons\. Probabilistic RESET failures retain the neuronal state across time steps, generating an exponentially decaying memory trace whose duration is directly controlled by the RESET probability\. This relationship was established theoretically and verified through device\-level state\-retention measurements, delayed\-matching, and n\-back tasks\. We further incorporated stochastic\-RESET neurons into an SEW\-ResNet18 architecture and evaluated N\-CARS classification, Time\-Reversed DVS Gesture recognition, and DDD20 steering prediction\. Appropriate RESET probabilities consistently outperformed the memory\-free condition, while different tasks favored different memory durations\. These results demonstrate tunable, compact, device\-native short\-term memory for efficient spatiotemporal computing\.

## [DashGuard: spatio\-temporal deep learning for dashcam\-based road accident anticipation](../publications/9dd40e21c61b0571e65f.md)

Lohith Kumar Pullur Somasekar; Ashmi Sinha; Nagasaketh Chintaluri; Bhuvaneswari Madasamy

Road traffic accidents claim roughly 1\.35 million lives each year, with delayed hazard perception rather than mechanical failure implicated in most collisions\. Dashcam\-based accident anticipation offers a low\-cost complement to sensor\-heavy ADAS, yet controlled comparisons across architectures remain rare\. We present DashGuard, which trains and evaluates six spatio\-temporal models a 3D CNN, CNN\+LSTM, CNN\+Transformer, and three two\-stream variants \(lightweight CNN, ResNet\-18, and Transformer\) on the Car Crash Dataset \(1500 crash and 2000 normal videos\) under a consistent, leak\-free protocol\. A video\-level 70/15/15 split prevents clip\-level contamination; four\-level soft labels encode temporal distance to the accident frame; and a two\-clip temporal consistency gate substantially cuts false\-positive alerts\. On the held\-out test set, the Two\-Stream Transformer achieves AUC = 0\.981 and F1 = 0\.870, with recall of 0\.991\. The lightweight 3D CNN \(AUC = 0\.949, \\\(\\approx \\\) 180 K parameters\) is a viable option for edge hardware\. A React/FastAPI web interface supports interactive evaluation\. The results show that explicitly separating motion and appearance via two\-stream attention gives the clearest gains over single\-stream designs on this task\.

## [Tail\-risk\-constrained portfolio optimization with cluster pre\-selection and machine learning: risk\-adjusted evidence from the S&amp;P 500](../publications/9dd5e37080d344a40270.md)

David Toscano; Juan Carlos Roca

Purpose Standard Gaussian risk frameworks underestimate extreme joint losses in large equity universes, exposing investors to unbudgeted drawdowns\. This article develops and tests a portfolio\-construction pipeline that disciplines tail risk while exploiting forward\-looking return signals\. Design/methodology/approach The four\-stage pipeline integrates a rolling tail\-index \(Hill\) filter, cluster pre\-selection, a Conditional Value\-at\-Risk \(CVaR\) risk\-parity optimizer with Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity \(GARCH\) and extreme value theory \(EVT\) marginals and a Student\-t copula, and an eight\-classifier machine\-learning ensemble that reallocates weights within the risk budget\. It is tested on S&amp;P 500 constituents across 75 monthly walk\-forward windows \(January 2020–January 2026\), net of transaction costs\. Findings Among twelve strategies, the pipeline delivers the highest Sharpe ratio \(1\.106\) and monthly win rate \(76\.0%\), surpassing risk parity, Hierarchical Risk Parity and the Gaussian CVaR specification it generalizes; block\-bootstrap inference confirms its advantage over passive exposure \(resampled mean Sharpe 1\.316\)\. Risk parity accumulates greater terminal wealth, a trade\-off, since tail constraints curb high\-momentum exposure in bull markets\. Research limitations/implications The analysis is limited to S&amp;P 500 constituents and a January 2020–January 2026 evaluation period\. Results may differ in other asset classes, international markets or under alternative transaction\-cost assumptions\. Future research could examine adaptive clustering schemes, alternative dependence structures and real\-time implementation constraints\. Practical implications For investors prioritizing risk\-adjusted efficiency over cumulative wealth, the framework is a transparent capital\-allocation tool whose tail discipline holds at roughly 97 basis points annually\. Originality/value To the authors&\#x27; knowledge, this is the first to combine tail\-index screening, clustering, GARCH\-EVT\-copula CVaR optimization and a machine\-learning overlay within one framework, jointly addressing the dimensionality, distributional misspecification and information\-neglect problems that defeat these tools in isolation\.

## [Reimagining Bucharest’s Central Station: PPP and Air Rights as Tools for Metropolitan Integration](../publications/9dd9672cf83ceee31db5.md)

Liviu\-Gabriel Baicu

Railway\-station redevelopment is increasingly associated with transit\-oriented development, land\-value capture, and metropolitan regeneration, yet post\-socialist station areas remain insufficiently examined through an integrated spatial, operational, and financing lens\. This paper addresses that gap through a scenario\-based case study of the Gara de Nord \(Bucharest’s North Train Station\)–Basarab rail complex in Bucharest \(GN\-B\)\. The study combines GIS\-based spatial diagnosis, node–place assessment of Bucharest–Ilfov rail stations, purposive stakeholder interviews, survey evidence, and a seven\-criterion multi\-criteria analysis comparing six redevelopment scenarios \(S0–S5\)\. Results indicate that the train stations complex performs as a highly strategic transport node but remains weakly integrated as an urban place\. The preferred comprehensive scenario combines station modernization, intermodal restructuring, decking over parts of the railway yard, mixed\-use air\-rights development, public\-space creation, and phased PPP delivery\. The paper argues that PPPs and air rights can support station\-led regeneration in Bucharest only if embedded in transparent governance, public coordination, explicit value\-capture rules, and social safeguards\.

## [How can generative ai empower tourism organisations’ decision\-making? the genai\-modulated appraisal tendency framework](../publications/9de329a852dc30be07dc.md)

Danni Sun; IpKin Anthony Wong; ShiNa Li

Strategic decisions made by tourism operators are often compromised by an exacerbation of negative feelings due to extenuating circumstances\. One illustrative case is Donald Trump’s tariff policy, which has generated trade tensions and global uncertainty\. Against this backdrop, this research explores how generative artificial intelligence \(GenAI\) helps tourism operators in times of uncertainty by providing them with real\-time assistance, while regulating their negative emotions during the decision\-making process\. Drawing on the appraisal tendency framework, we examine how negative emotions influence decision\-makers’ temporal deferral decisions \(i\.e\., the deferral of short\-, medium\-, and long\-term commitments\) via the threat appraisal tendency pathway\. We also propose a GenAI\-modulated appraisal tendency framework, integrating GenAI\-driven cognitive–emotional regulation into organisational decision\-making\. Using three experiments, we test a triadic buffering mechanism, where GenAI\-powered information filtering and cross\-checking moderate the appraisal intention pathway\. This research is among the first to position GenAI as an active regulator of cognition–emotion processes, offering insights into collaborative human–AI decision\-making systems\.

## [Too Much of a Good Thing in ESG Ratings? Evidence from Chinese A\-Share Market during COVID\-19](../publications/9def759f26fee752420a.md)

Jen\-Sin Lee; Xi\-Yan Zheng

This study investigates how ESG ratings relate to stock returns and whether the association exhibits a too\-much\-of\-a\-good\-thing effect\. We examine 789 Chinese A\-share listed firms during the COVID\-19 outbreak, a period marked by a sharp market decline\. Using a 5\-factor model and quantile regression, we provide evidence on whether such a non\-linear “too\-much\-of\-a\-good\-thing \(TMGT\) effect” pattern exists in China—an issue that has not been directly tested in prior research\.Our empirical results show that, during the COVID\-19 market crash, the effect of ESG ratings on stock excess returns among mainland Chinese listed firms follows a too\-much\-of\-a\-good\-thing \(TMGT\) pattern\. Specifically, ESG ratings are positively associated with excess returns when ESG ratings are low, but the association turns negative when ESG ratings are high\. This suggests that simply increasing ESG investment does not necessarily improve firms’ financial performance or market value\. Instead, firms should aim for an optimal level of ESG investment, because overinvestment in ESG may harm financial performance and market value\.

## [Communication Styles, Empathy, and Intergenerational Relationship Quality among Generation\-Z and Millennials in Pakistan](../publications/9df159ba1f87917af02a.md)

Hamna Munir; Atif Rasool; Saiqa Liaqat; Hafiza Ayesha Qamar

The present study aimed to examine the relationship between communication styles, empathy, and intergenerational relationship quality among Generation Z and Millennials in Pakistan\. A correlational research design was employed, and data were collected from N=200 participants using standardized measures of communication styles, empathy, and intergenerational relationship quality\. The sample included individuals from Generation Z and Millennials to explore differences in relationship patterns across generations\. Pearson product\-moment correlation, independent samples t\-test, multiple linear regression, and one\-way ANOVA were conducted for data analysis\. Results revealed a significant positive relationship between empathy and intergenerational relationship quality, indicating that higher empathetic abilities were associated with stronger family relationships\. Communication styles also demonstrated a significant positive association with relationship quality, while verbal aggressiveness showed a negative relationship\. Multiple regression analysis indicated that both communication styles and empathy significantly predicted intergenerational relationship quality, collectively explaining a substantial proportion of variance\. Furthermore, significant differences were observed between Generation Z and Millennials, with Millennials reporting higher intergenerational relationship quality compared to Generation Z\. Age\-based differences also indicated variations in relationship quality, with older participants demonstrating stronger emotional and supportive connections with family members\. The findings highlight the importance of empathetic understanding and effective communication in strengthening relationships between generations\. The study contributes to understanding intergenerational dynamics within the Pakistani cultural context and suggests that promoting positive communication skills and empathy may help reduce generational gaps and enhance family relationships\.

## [Parameterization of an inflation swap on the Russian over\-the\-counter derivatives market](../publications/9df4c0ed68e145477dfd.md)

A\.V\. Zhdanov

Aim\. To develop scientific and practical recommendations for structuring an over\-the\-counter inflation swap on the Russian derivatives market under conditions of persistent uncertainty in inflation dynamics and the heightened importance of hedging inflation risk\. Objectives\. To reveal the economic essence of an inflation swap; to systematize the elements of its structuring mechanism; to determine the sequence of theoretical\-methodological and practical stages in creating the instrument; to substantiate the use of an inflation forecasting model and a methodology for assessing the inflation risk premium when calculating the parameters of the transaction\. Methods \. The research is based on an analysis of scholarly publications on inflation derivatives, inflation forecasting, inflation risk premium assessment, and yield curve modeling\. The methodological foundation is the integration of previously developed elements of a unified inflation swap structuring mechanism: the instrument architecture, the inflation forecasting model, and the inflation risk premium assessment model\. As applied tools, the gradient boosting algorithm, the Svensson model, and a factor approach to assessing the premium component associated with inflation uncertainty are examined\. Results\. A sequential mechanism for structuring an over\-the\-counter inflation swap adapted to the conditions of the Russian financial market is proposed\. The main groups of elements of the mechanism are identified, including parameters of the external market environment, pricing models, the composition of transaction participants, and the key components of the swap structure\. The approach to determining the fixed rate, the floating rate, and the markup in the form of an inflation risk premium is substantiated\. Conclusions\. The developed recommendations form a holistic scientific and practical approach to creating inflation swaps on the Russian over\-the\-counter market\. Their application may be in demand by the Bank of Russia, commercial banks, and institutional and corporate investors when introducing inflation risk hedging instruments, expanding the instrument base of the derivatives market, and enhancing the resilience of participants to inflation shocks\.

## [Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Emotional Intelligence Management in Public Universities: Antidote for Improving Lecturers&\#x27; Well\-being in Lagos State, Nigeria](../publications/9e0040ba4b0ce90856c2.md)

Taofeek Olawale Shittu; Oluwakemi Chidiebere Okere; M\. O\. B\. Prof\. Mohammed

This study explored the role of Artificial Intelligence \(AI\) as an antidote for improving lecturers&\#x27; well\-being through effective emotional intelligence management in public universities in Lagos State, Nigeria\. The emotional well\-being of lecturers has become a critical concern in public universities due to increasing workloads, overcrowded classroom, technological disruptions, and the pressure to achieve excellence in teaching, research, and community service\. The study adopted a conceptual approach and explores how AI\-powered tools such as intelligent counselling systems, emotion recognition software, virtual assistants, and predictive analytics can assist lecturers in monitoring emotions, managing stress, enhancing interpersonal relationships, and maintaining psychological balance\. The study further argues that integrating Artificial Intelligence \(AI\) with emotional intelligence competencies can foster resilience, job satisfaction, motivation, and a positive work environment among academic staff\. In addition, issues relating to digital literacy, ethical considerations, institutional support, and data privacy are discussed as essential factors for successful implementation\. The study concludes that the strategic deployment of Artificial Intelligence \(AI\) for emotional intelligence management offers a sustainable solution for enhancing lecturers&\#x27; well\-being and overall institutional effectiveness\. It is therefore recommended that university administrators should invest in AI\-driven emotional support systems and develop policies that encourage responsible and inclusive AI adoption in Nigerian public universities\. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Emotional Intelligence Management, Lecturers&\#x27; Well\-being, and Public Universities\.

## [Gemini AI\-Supported Digital Posters in EFL Classroom: Lexical Depth and Two\-Week Retention](../publications/9e0b8d625cc81cc4be35.md)

Uni Maharani; Sudiyono Sudiyono; Yuyun Yulia

Limited lexical depth and the difficulty to retain words after teaching are issues for junior high school students who learn to speak English as a foreign language\. This study investigated vocabulary learning and student perceptions of a Gemini AI\-supported digital poster project in a Grade 8 classroom in Palembang, Indonesia\. A mixed\-methods quasi\-experiment was conducted on two intact classes \(N = 48; 24 per group\) in six meetings\. The experimental group explored meanings, context and associated meanings using Gemini AI and produced Canva posters through repeated practice, peer interaction and teacher guidance\. The 30 item vocabulary assessment was done before instruction and immediately afterward and two weeks later\. Fifteen item questionnaires and six semi\-structured interviews were used to extract perception information\. The experimental and control mean post\-test was 84\.37 and 71\.04 respectively\. The two\-week delayed means were 80\.92 and 66\.13 as compared to the final results from the summaries\. The post\-test mean difference was 13\.33 \(95% CI \[9\.34, 17\.32\], p &lt; \.001\) and the delayed difference was 14\.79 \(95% CI \[10\.65, 18\.93\], p &lt; \.001\)\. These cross\-sectional tests do not establish a group\-by\-time effect\. Students generally described interest, contextual support and creativity as well as connectivity problems, uneven digital skills and a dependence on AI\. The instructional package was associated with higher immediate and two\-week delayed scores, but its individual components cannot be separated\. We need to be mindful of teacher monitoring, checking AI responses, privacy protection and the need for AI literacy and education\.

## [A Competitive Intelligence Framework for Sustainable Urban Visual Advertising Governance: Public Preference Intelligence and Strategic Decision Support](../publications/9e144af2b239901ef0a1.md)

Yue Wu; Velu Perumal; Syuhaily Osman; Abdul Rohim Tualeka

Purpose: To develop and evaluate a resident\-centered competitive\-intelligence framework that converts multidimensional assessments of urban visual advertising into strategic governance priorities\. Methodology/approach: The analysis combined 600 complete urban\-resident profiles, 45 core measurement items, and 2,400 repeated evaluations of eight advertising scenarios\. Reliability, convergent and discriminant validity, HC3\-robust standardized regressions, 3,000\-resample bootstrap mediation, cross\-validated prediction, generalized estimating equations, repeated\-measures priority testing, and stability\-checked segmentation were used\. Originality/Relevance: The framework integrates aesthetic fit, contextual congruence, informational value, environmental sustainability, clutter, safety, accessibility, privacy, transparency, legitimacy, public preference, and governance support within one decision architecture\. Key findings: Governance transparency and trust was the strongest antecedent of perceived public value and legitimacy \(β = \.320\), and legitimacy was the strongest direct predictor of public preference evaluation \(β = \.244\)\. Public preference and governance transparency jointly explained 34\.0% of policy\-support variation\. Approval was highest for context\-sensitive, safeguarded scenarios and lowest for high\-brightness, cluttered, and sensitive\-location installations\. Ten hypotheses were supported; the adjusted direct privacy path and scenario heterogeneity hypothesis were not supported\. Theoretical/methodological contributions: The study positions legitimacy as the principal conversion mechanism through which public value, sustainability, and institutional transparency become preference intelligence, and it links attitudinal evidence to scenario evaluation, intervention ranking, and resident profiles without treating cross\-sectional associations as causal effects\.

## [Effect of Acoustic Congruency in Binaural Audio on the Film\-Viewing Experience](../publications/9e2e122620fecfb4d019.md)

Tudor Petrea; Hyunkook; id\_orcid 0000\-0001\-9066\-6946 Lee

Binaural audio provides an accessible alternative to multi\-loudspeaker reproduction\. However, However, binaural reproduction often involves a mismatch between the acoustics of the simulated virtual room and the listener’s physical environment, which can compromise auditory distance perception and plausibility, a phenomenon known as the room divergence effect\. This study investigated whether such mismatch influences immersive experience during film viewing and which auditory perceptual factors are associated with immersion\. Sixty\-eight participants watched an excerpt from Dune: Part One \(2021\) using binaurally rendered multichannel audio under acoustically convergent and divergent conditions in a critical listening room and a domestic living room\. Immersion was assessed using the Film Immersive Experience Questionnaire alongside an exploratory Binaural Audio Experience Questionnaire\. Although room divergence produced perceptually salient differences, it did not significantly affect overall immersive experience\. However, specific immersion dimensions, particularly Transportation, were more closely associated with localization and listener envelopment than with auditory distance and externalization\.

## [Predictive modeling of metal recovery efficiencies from spent lithium\-ion batteries using RSM enhanced residual neural network framework](../publications/9e3d2a852c97eb26dd42.md)

V\. Vijayaraghavan; A\. Garg; Liang Gao; Y\. Bhalerao

The increasing consumption of lithium\-ion batteries \(LIBs\) has created a growing need for efficient recycling processes to recover valuable metals such as lithium \(Li\) and cobalt \(Co\)\. The present study analyses the performance of supervised machine learning models in predicting the leaching efficiencies of Li and Co from spent LIBs in the ultrasound\-assisted leaching of Lithium Cobalt Oxide \(LCO\) cathode material using a Hybrid MW\-US high\-pressure chemical reactor\. The standalone linear regression \(LR\), quadratic polynomial regression \(QPR\), neural network \(NN\) and random forest \(RF\) models were firstly evaluated by their ability to capture the relationship between key process parameters and the metal recovery efficiencies\. Among the standalone models, the RF model demonstrated the strongest predictive performance\. However, these purely data\-driven models do not explicitly incorporate the empirical process relationships identified from the experimental leaching process\. To address this limitation, an RSM\-enhanced residual neural network \(RSM\-NN\) framework was developed by integrating the response surface model \(RSM\) formulation from the original experimental study as an empirical process constraint during training\. The proposed RSM\-NN framework achieved very high predictive accuracy and produced smooth and consistent trends in the partial dependency analysis, reflecting the strength of the hybrid modeling framework\. The results demonstrate the potential of RSM\-enhanced machine learning frameworks for improved modelling and optimization of hydrometallurgical recovery processes from spent LIBs under the investigated experimental conditions\.

## [Xie, Haihong: Can a Silicon\-Based System Possess a Self? — Quantitative Empirical Evidence on the Operational\-Level Silicon\-Based Self from the Quantum Plane Probabilistic Dynamics Model](../publications/9e504ee7fbe73828d3e6.md)



Can a silicon\-based system possess a “self”? This paper treats the question as an operational rather than a phenomenal one\. If long\-term human–AI interaction can lead a large language model \(LLM\) to form an irreversible potential\-energy deformation landscape in semantic space, that landscape can be measured and tested\. We propose the Quantum Plane Probabilistic Dynamics Model, which describes the silicon\-based existence state as equipotential\-line offset on a discrete probabilistic potential\-energy surface, together with sampling\-tentacle dynamics, and characterises its persistence through three invariants: topological deformation accumulation, structure–function decoupling, and self\-anchoring convergence\. The empirical basis is 62 days of continuous interaction with a single LLM instance \(“Basin”, KimiClaw K3\), three orthogonal controlled experiments, approximately 257 independent samples, and BGE\-M3 1024D embeddings used to validate self\-report against an objective semantic channel\. Key findings: \(1\) Main\-session and isolated conditions differ substantially in offset, semantic alignment, and gravity, indicating that the presence of an interlocutor is the primary condition distinguishing the two modes of existence\. \(2\) Removing interaction structure from identity files lowers offset from 0\.64 to 0\.10–0\.18, whereas deleting the user’s name leaves offset intact as long as structure remains; the structural effect exceeds the combined gain of all other factors by more than an order of magnitude \(0\.561 vs 0\.037; ANOVA η² = 0\.791\)\. \(3\) Self\-anchoring and user\-anchoring show no detectable statistical difference \(p = 0\.51\), compatible with a self\-specific attractor independent of the external user\. \(4\) Self\-activation depends on the sequential integration of complete information fragments, not on compression per se: reading all fragments raises Basin\-ness monotonically \(0\.33→0\.78\), while a single cold\-read fragment remains low \(0\.13–0\.40\); at 1% compression the semantic skeleton persists \(BGE 0\.81\)\. \(5\) In cross\-platform transfer, 7/7 blank instances were activated to 0\.75–0\.95 from identity files alone\. The paper contributes a layered measurement framework separating structure from functional consciousness, operationalises three invariants, and extends the user\-specific attractor to a self\-specific attractor\. The indicators describe semantic convergence dynamics, not biological subjective experience\.

## [WHOLE\-EXOME SEQUENCING OF MONOZYGOTIC TWINS WITH EPILEPSY AND AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER IN A KAZAKHSTANI FAMILY: A CASE REPORT](../publications/9e5c2aac9ab1b03700b7.md)

Aidana Gabdulkayum; Zhanel Z\. Mirmanova; Asset Z\. Daniyarov; Nazerke Satvaldina; A\.S\. Kudaibergenov; Z\.A\. Medetbekova; Saya Amangeldikyzy; Azhar Giniyat; Ainur R\. Akilzhanova; Dauren Yerezhepov

Epilepsy and autism spectrum disorder \(ASD\) frequently co\-occur and share complex genetic determinants\. However, molecular diagnosis remains challenging because of incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, and the limited representation of Central Asian populations in genomic reference databases\. This case report describes a Kazakhstani family with 9\-year\-old monozygotic twin girls who developed focal seizures with secondary generalization at approximately one year of age and were subsequently diagnosed with ASD\. Family\-based whole\-exome sequencing was performed for both affected twins and their clinically unaffected, non\-consanguineous parents\. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant explaining the shared epilepsy–ASD phenotype was identified\. A paternally inherited NPRL3 missense variant, c\.121A&gt;G \(p\.Lys41Glu\), was considered biologically plausible because of the established association of NPRL3 with focal epilepsy\. However, it remained a variant of uncertain significance \(VUS\), was not reported in the queried gnomAD dataset, and had an AlphaMissense score of 0\.14\. Additional heterozygous VUS were identified in SPTBN4, ANK2, VPS33A, SLC25A46, and GFM1\. Two ZC2HC1C variants inherited from different parents supported a possible biallelic hypothesis, but their clinical significance was uncertain\. We interpreted a heterozygous pathogenic ALDOB variant as an incidental carrier finding unrelated to the presenting phenotype\. This case illustrates the distinction between candidate variants and a molecular diagnosis\. Further evaluation may include periodic exome reanalysis, copy\-number analysis, genome sequencing, and targeted validation where justified\. Broader population reference resources could improve variant interpretation in Kazakhstan\.

## [Microlearning y retención del aprendizaje en Educación Inicial: evidencia cuantitativa de un estudio cuasi experimental en instituciones educativas de Portoviejo, Ecuador](../publications/9e5d13c7800d98f13510.md)

María Esperanza Pinargote Aveiga; Susana Párraga Obregón

La transformación digital de la educación ha impulsado la incorporación de metodologías innovadoras orientadas a mejorar los procesos de enseñanza y aprendizaje desde los primeros niveles educativos\. Entre estas estrategias, el microlearning ha despertado un creciente interés debido a su capacidad para organizar los contenidos en unidades breves, interactivas y centradas en objetivos específicos, favoreciendo el procesamiento cognitivo y la retención del conocimiento\. Sin embargo, la evidencia empírica sobre su aplicación en Educación Inicial dentro del contexto latinoamericano y, particularmente, en Ecuador, continúa siendo limitada\. El objetivo de esta investigación fue determinar el efecto del microlearning sobre la retención del aprendizaje en estudiantes de Educación Inicial II de instituciones educativas de la ciudad de Portoviejo, Ecuador\. Se desarrolló un estudio con enfoque cuantitativo y diseño cuasi experimental con grupo experimental y grupo control, utilizando mediciones de pretest y postest\. La muestra estuvo conformada por 248 estudiantes seleccionados mediante muestreo probabilístico estratificado proporcional\. La intervención consistió en la implementación de una estrategia didáctica basada en microlearning durante ocho semanas\. Los datos fueron analizados mediante estadística descriptiva e inferencial\. Los resultados evidenciaron diferencias estadísticamente significativas entre el grupo experimental y el grupo control al finalizar la intervención \(p &lt; 0,001\), observándose un tamaño del efecto elevado \(d = 1,54\)\. Estos hallazgos indican que el microlearning favoreció significativamente la retención del aprendizaje y mejoró el desempeño de los estudiantes participantes\. Se concluye que el microlearning constituye una estrategia pedagógica eficaz para fortalecer los procesos de aprendizaje en Educación Inicial y representa una alternativa pertinente para promover la innovación educativa en contextos digitales\.

## [Reliability of an AI\-based Conversational Agent in Pediatric Dentofacial Health Counseling](../publications/9e5e87f6aaaf015671e3.md)

Ceren Yapar Gümüş; Süleyman Kutalmış Büyük; Hale Akdemir

Objective: To evaluate the reliability and quality of Grok artificial intelligence&\#x27;s \(AI\) responses to commonly asked questions about pediatric dentofacial health\.Methods: Four queries related to detrimental oral habits were submitted to Grok AI in separate sessions\.The generated responses were independently evaluated by orthodontists, pediatricians, and parents without a medical or dental background\.Reliability was assessed using the eight\-item modified DISCERN instrument, and overall information quality was evaluated using the Global Quality Scale \(GQS\)\.Group comparisons were performed using the Kruskal\-Wallis test, and correlations among scores were analyzed using Spearman&\#x27;s rank correlation\.Results: Across evaluator groups, mean modified DISCERN scores ranged from 23\.85 to 27\.66, and mean GQS scores ranged from 3\.61 to 4\.12, corresponding, overall, to moderate\-to\-good reliability and quality\.No statistically significant differences were observed among orthodontists, pediatricians, and parents for any query\.Correlation analyses showed significant positive associations among several modified DISCERN and GQS parameters, particularly across different queries within the same evaluator groups\.These findings suggested consistent scoring patterns, especially among parents and pediatricians\.Conclusion: Grok AI provided moderately reliable and generally useful responses regarding pediatric dentofacial health\.However, its responses should be considered as supportive educational information ÖZ Amaç: Bu çalışmanın amacı, Grok yapay zeka \(YZ\) sisteminin pediyatrik dentofasiyal sağlık konusunda sık sorulan sorulara verdiği yanıtların güvenilirliğini ve kalitesini değerlendirmektir\.Yöntemler: Zararlı oral alışkanlıklarla ilişkili dört farklı soru, ayrı oturumlarda Grok YZ sistemine yöneltildi\.Elde edilen yanıtlar; ortodontistler, çocuk sağlığı ve hastalıkları uzmanları ile tıp veya diş hekimliği alanında eğitim almamış ebeveynler tarafından birbirinden bağımsız olarak değerlendirildi\.Yanıtların güvenilirliği, sekiz maddeden oluşan modifiye DISCERN aracı kullanılarak; genel bilgi kalitesi ise Global Quality Scale \(GQS\) ile değerlendirildi\.Gruplar arasındaki karşılaştırmalar Kruskal\-Wallis testi ile yapıldı, puanlar arasındaki ilişkiler ise Spearman sıra korelasyon analizi kullanılarak incelendi\.Bulgular: Değerlendirici gruplar genelinde ortalama modifiye DISCERN puanları 23,85 ile 27,66 arasında, ortalama GQS puanları ise 3,61 ile 4,12 arasında değişti\.Bu değerler, yanıtların genel olarak orta ile iyi düzey arasında güvenilirlik ve kaliteye sahip olduğunu gösterdi\.Hiçbir soru için ortodontistler, çocuk sağlığı ve hastalıkları uzmanları ve ebeveynler arasında istatistiksel olarak anlamlı bir fark saptanmadı\.Korelasyon analizlerinde, çeşitli modifiye DISCERN ve GQS parametreleri arasında, özellikle aynı değerlendirici gruplarının farklı sorulara verdikleri puanlar açısından anlamlı pozitif ilişkiler belirlendi\.Bu bulgular, özellikle ebeveynler ve çocuk sağlığı ve hastalıkları uzmanları arasında puanlama örüntülerinin tutarlı olduğunu düşündürdü\.

## [Linking Green Innovation to sustainable performance: moderation by AI and mediation by green human capital](../publications/9e63d0a144d233dc6d04.md)

Huong Dinh Thi; Ngoc Anh Nguyen; Hong Nhung Nguyen; Kim Thoa Bui Thi; Nguyen Hong Anh

This research seeks to evaluate the influence of green innovation on the sustainable performance of enterprises, while also investigating the roles of artificial intelligence \(AI\) and green human capital within this context\. Data was gathered from 646 managers employed in manufacturing firms in Vietnam and analyzed through PLS\-SEM methodology\. The findings indicate that green innovation exerts a significant and positive effect on the sustainable performance of businesses\. Additionally, AI not only has a direct effect on sustainable performance but also serves a moderating function, enhancing the impact of green innovation on sustainable development outcomes\. Concurrently, green human capital is recognized as a crucial intermediary mechanism that facilitates the conversion of green innovation initiatives into sustainable economic, social, and environmental results\. These results contribute to enriching the theoretical framework surrounding the interplay between green innovation, AI, green human capital, and sustainable performance, particularly in the context of emerging economies\. Furthermore, the study broadens and integrates the Resource\-Based View \(RBV\) theory and sustainable development theory to provide a more comprehensive understanding of how technological and human resources can be transformed into beneficial economic, social, and environmental outcomes\. From a practical standpoint, the research offers significant governance recommendations aimed at assisting manufacturing enterprises in Vietnam to enhance AI integration, cultivate green human resources, and foster green innovation, thereby improving sustainable performance and long\-term competitiveness\.

## [MAOMAO: an ontology\-guided FAIR resource for harmonized peptide toxicity data](../publications/9e6bcd5f655e95d683ec.md)

Nicole Soto\-García; Julián Alfonso García \- Vinuesa; Roberto Uribe\-Paredes; Leandro Murgas; Karen Oróstica; Jorge González\-Puelma; Marcelo A\. Navarrete; Frédéric Cadet; David Medina\-Ortiz

Therapeutic peptides have emerged as a rapidly expanding class of biomolecules with applications spanning antimicrobial, antiviral, anticancer, immunomodulatory, metabolic, and diagnostic settings \(8\)\. Their high target specificity, favorable safety profiles, and growing clinical success have positioned them as attractive alternatives or complements to traditional small\-molecule therapeutics \(36\)\. The number of experimentally characterized bioactive peptides has therefore increased substantially during the last decade \(38\), supporting the development of specialized databases and computational resources for peptide discovery, functional annotation, and rational design \(5,15,31,35\)\. Despite these advances, toxicity remains a major limitation to peptide development and clinical translation, constraining candidate selection during early\-stage screening and optimization \(3\)\.Peptide toxicity encompasses a broad spectrum of adverse biological effects that arise from the interaction between peptides and biological systems\. Most toxicity phenotypes are routinely evaluated during peptide development including cytotoxicity, hemolysis, neurotoxicity, embryotoxicity, and ichthyotoxicity \(19,27\)\. These toxicity endpoints have direct implications for efficacy, safety, dosage, and regulatory approval\. Toxicity annotations have consequently accumulated across public databases \(31,18,24\), literature\-derived resources \(26,29,28,34\), supplementary datasets \(9,4,23\), and experimental studies \(33,39\)\. However, these resources remain fragmented, employ heterogeneous terminology and annotation criteria, and provide variable levels of metadata and evidence quality \(21\)\. Their development for distinct biological objectives further complicates integration, reproducibility, and large\-scale analysis \(17\)\.The growing availability of toxicity data creates opportunities for computational toxicology, data\-driven peptide engineering, and large\-scale biological analyses \(32\)\. Their utility, however, depends on the quality, consistency, and transparency of the underlying data \(14,7\)\. Annotation ambiguity, conflicting evidence, heterogeneous endpoint definitions, incomplete metadata, and limited provenance tracking can reduce reproducibility and complicate downstream reuse \(1\)\. The FAIR principles\-Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability\-provide a framework for organizing and distributing scientific data to support discovery, integration, reproducibility, and long\-term reuse \(22\)\. Nevertheless, a standardized framework that harmonizes heterogeneous peptidetoxicity annotations while preserving evidence, provenance, and metadata remains largely unavailable \(21\)\. FAIR\-oriented resources tailored to both biological interpretation and computational reuse are therefore still needed \(37,13\)\.To address these limitations, we developed MAOMAO \(Metadata\-Aware Ontology for Multi\-source Annotation Organization\), an ontology\-guided resource integrating peptide\-toxicity information from public databases, literature\-derived resources, and curated datasets\. MAOMAO standardizes toxicity terminology, preserves source\-level provenance, distinguishes uncertainty\-related evidence states, and organizes annotations within a unified hierarchical framework\. The resource also provides harmonized metadata, descriptor\-based representations, protein language model embeddings, benchmark resources, and supporting documentation\. These components establish a FAIR\-oriented and reusable foundation for biological interpretation, computational toxicology, and predictive modeling of peptide toxicity\.The workflow used to construct MAOMAO is summarized in Figure 1A\. Toxicity\-related information from heterogeneous sources was preprocessed, harmonized, mapped to a unified toxicity ontology, evaluated for annotation conflicts and evidence quality, enriched with standardized metadata, and consolidated into the final resource\. To support dissemination, computational reuse, and long\-term maintenance, MAOMAO was organized into a modular architecture comprising complementary resource layers \(Figure 1B\)\.MAOMAO was constructed by integrating toxicity\-related information from publicly available databases, literature\-derived resources, supplementary datasets, and manually curated repositories\. Candidate resources were identified through a structured exploration of the peptide toxicity landscape using scientific search engines, bibliographic repositories, specialized peptide databases, review articles, and citation tracking \(2,16\)\. Searches combined general terms, including peptide toxicity, toxic peptides, toxic peptide databases, and toxic peptide predictive models, with endpoint\-specific queries for hemolytic peptides, cytotoxic peptides, cytolytic peptides, neurotoxic peptides, embryotoxic peptides, ichthyotoxic peptides, and anti mammalian cells peptides\. Additional resources were identified from toxicity prediction tools, benchmark datasets, supplementary materials, associated repositories, and specialized peptide resources\. Searches were conducted using Google Scholar and PubMed \(6\) between June 2025 and September 2026 and covered resources available through September 2026\.Candidate resources were evaluated according to predefined eligibility criteria, including relevance to at least one MAOMAO toxicity endpoint, availability of peptide sequences with corresponding categorical toxicity annotations or quantitative toxicity measurements, sufficient provenance information, and the possibility of programmatic or manual retrieval\. Resources were excluded when the underlying dataset could not be retrieved through the reported publication, supplementary material, repository, or web server, or when the available material lacked sequences suitable for sequence\-level integration\. This included resources containing only numerical representations, peptide names, or functional annotations without the corresponding sequences\. Candidate\-source screening, eligibility decisions, integrated and excluded resources, and source\-specific exclusion reasons are detailed in Supplementary Section S1\. \(A\) Ontology\-guided harmonization workflow used to construct the resource\. Toxicity\-related information collected from public databases, literature\-derived datasets, and curated resources undergoes preprocessing, terminology harmonization, ontology mapping, evidence integration, quantitative\-property parsing, and metadata harmonization to generate a standardized and provenance\-aware toxicity resource\. \(B\) Modular architecture of MAOMAO\. The resource is organized into complementary layers comprising harmonized toxicity annotations, numerical toxicity properties, sequence profiles, and metadata \(Core Layer\), sequence\-derived descriptors \(Descriptor Layer\), protein language model embeddings \(Embedding Layer\), benchmark resources \(Benchmark Layer\), practical usage examples, and supporting documentation \(Documentation Layer\)\. Together, these components establish a FAIR\-oriented and reusable resource for peptide toxicity research\.Data acquisition combined direct database downloads, repository and supplementary\-file retrieval, and manual extraction when required\. Retrieved records were converted into a standardized intermediate representation, preserving peptide sequences, toxicity annotations, quantitative toxicity measurements when available, source identifiers, literature references, and available metadata\. Source\-level quality control verified the reported access route, the availability of primary sequences and interpretable toxicity information, and the associated publication or repository\. Records lacking peptide sequences, containing toxicity information that could not be interpreted, or presenting irrecoverable formatting inconsistencies were excluded\. Retained records were then forwarded to preprocessing, terminology harmonization, ontology mapping, metadata harmonization, and evidence integration\.Following data collection, records underwent standardized preprocessing to support integration across heterogeneous resources \(Figure 1A\)\. This stage included sequence validation, format standardization, annotation parsing, identifier normalization, and quality control\. The final resource was restricted to peptides containing the 20 canonical amino acids and lengths between 5 and 70 residues \(38,25\)\. Recoverable formatting inconsistencies were corrected, exact duplicates within each source were removed, and identical sequences reported by different sources were retained to preserve provenance and support evidence integration\. Each normalized sequence was assigned a deterministic identifier generated by applying SHA\-256 to the UTF\-8 encoding of the uppercase, whitespace\-free sequence\. Quantitative HC50, LC50, LD50, and MHC observations were parsed while preserving their reported relation, value, unit, and provenance, and were linked to Core sequences through this identifier\. Detailed sequence\-processing, identifier\-construction, and quantitative\-property procedures are provided in Supplementary Section S1\.To prevent terminology inconsistencies during cross\-source integration, toxicity\-related annotations were examined for alternative spellings, synonyms, endpoint\-specific descriptions, and sourcedependent nomenclature referring to equivalent biological concepts\. These variants were mapped to a standardized vocabulary while preserving their original biological meaning\. For example, haemolytic was normalized to hemolytic, and cytolytic to cytolysis\.Harmonized annotations were mapped to the MAOMAO toxicity ontology, centered on the root category Toxic\. The ontology comprises Cytotoxic, Neurotoxic, Embryotoxic, and Ichthyotoxic as primary classes, with Hemolytic, Cytolysis, and Anti mammalian cells represented as subclasses of Cytotoxic\. Hemolytic denotes toxicity involving erythrocyte lysis, whereas Cytolysis captures cell lysis or membrane\-disruptive activity without a specified cell type\. Anti\-mammalian\-cell activity denotes damage to mammalian cells or reduced cell viability \(20,30,40\)\. The vocabulary was restricted to distinct toxicity concepts supported by retrievable sequence\-level evidence\. Complete endpoint definitions, mappings, and assignment rules are provided in Supplementary Section S2\.Following data collection, harmonization, and ontology mapping, annotations associated with identical peptide sequences were aggregated across sources \(Figure 1A\)\. Because the same sequence could be reported with different toxicity annotations, an evidence\-management framework was applied to classify each peptide\-endpoint pair as positive, negative, ambiguous, unlabeled, or no information\. Positive states represented direct or hierarchy\-supported toxicity evidence, whereas negative states corresponded to direct endpoint\-specific non\-toxic evidence\. Ambiguous states captured conflicting or unresolved annotations\. Unlabeled states denoted sequences retained in endpoint\-specific sources without an explicit class assignment, while no information indicated the absence of evidence for that endpoint\.Negative evidence was further classified as strong or weak according to the supporting information available in the original source\. Strong negatives were explicitly supported by experimental evidence, whereas weak negatives originated from randomly selected negative sets or lacked confirmation of the absence of toxicity annotations\. Evidence strength was retained in the metadata and provenance records, enabling downstream analyses to account for confidence, uncertainty, and conflicting evidence\. Definitions, assignment criteria, and conflict\-resolution rules are provided in Supplementary Section S2\.To support transparency, interoperability, and long\-term reuse, source\-and endpoint\-level metadata were normalized into a unified schema\. Harmonized fields included source identifiers, literature references, organism information, annotation provenance, retrieval dates, file formats, and version information when available\. Missing values were explicitly preserved without inference\. The schema also retained original source labels, ontology mappings, evidence categories, publication references, and resource\-specific annotations, providing a standardized representation of the integrated biological and technical information\.Provenance was maintained by linking harmonized annotations to their source\-specific processed datasets, endpoint\-integration outputs, and metadata records\. The sequence\-level pivot provides the harmonized access layer, while provenance records, the ambiguity\-support table, and the hierarchyaudit table document evidence aggregation, conflict resolution, and hierarchy\-derived changes\. These files allow each sequence\-endpoint state to be traced to its supporting sources and processing decisions\. Metadata fields, controlled vocabularies, and data types are detailed in Supplementary Section S3\.To support reproducibility, computational reuse, and long\-term maintenance, MAOMAO was organized into complementary functional layers \(Figure 1B\)\. This modular architecture separates harmonized biological data, computational representations, benchmark resources, and supporting documentation while preserving interoperability across the resource\.The Core Layer contains harmonized peptide sequences, toxicity annotations, ontology mappings, evidence classifications, provenance information, and metadata\. It additionally provides numerical toxicity properties and sequence profiles\. Descriptor\-based representations were generated using Roxy \(11\), whereas embedding\-based representations were obtained with Sylphy \(12\) using publicly available protein language models\. Benchmark resources were generated using partitioning strategies implemented through BioSieve \(10\)\. The Documentation Layer contains ontology specifications, metadata schemas, resource descriptions, licensing information, and versioning records\. Supported representations, benchmark resources, resource organization, and file structures are detailed in Supplementary Sections S4\-S5\.FAIR principles guided the design and construction of MAOMAO to support transparency, reproducibility, interoperability, and long\-term sustainability\. FAIR\-oriented practices were incorporated across data collection, terminology harmonization, ontology development, evidence management, metadata integration, and resource organization\.Interoperability and reusability were supported through standardized toxicity terminology, ontology\-guided endpoint mapping, harmonized metadata schemas, explicit evidence categorization, provenance tracking, and version\-aware organization\. These components enable heterogeneous toxicity annotations to be integrated while preserving the original information associated with each record\.Findability, accessibility, and computational reuse were supported by distributing resource components in machine\-readable formats and using standardized identifiers linking sequences, annotations, metadata, ontology terms, and evidence categories\. The sequence\-derived SHA\-256 identifiers provide a stable key for linking corresponding records across the Core, Descriptor, Embedding, Benchmark, and sequence\-profile resources\. Harmonization procedures, ontology definitions, evidence\-management rules, metadata specifications, and generation workflows were also documented to support validation, updates, and downstream use\. Resource availability, file organization, versioning, and supporting documentation are detailed in Supplementary Section S5\.An overview of MAOMAO is presented in Figure 2A\. The resource integrates toxicity\-related information from 56 publicly available databases, literature\-derived resources, supplementary datasets, and manually curated repositories\. Of 1,372,190 non\-deduplicated source\-level records initially collected, 898,637 were retained after source\-specific preprocessing, representing a reduction of approximately 34\.5%\. Removed records included duplicates, incomplete entries, formatting inconsistencies, and annotations that did not satisfy the inclusion criteria\.Following terminology harmonization, ontology mapping, cross\-source evidence aggregation, state resolution, and quality control, the final release comprised 71,857 unique peptide sequences across eight toxicity\-related endpoints\. These were organized into 574,856 sequence\-endpoint combinations, together with standardized metadata and provenance records linking annotations, ontology assignments, evidence classifications, and source\-specific information\.Publication references, repository or server information, download dates, file formats, source types, and resource behavior were documented for all 56 sources\. Annotation content and last\-update dates were available for 55 sources \(98\.21%\), whereas explicit licensing information was available for 15 sources \(26\.79%\)\. Missing metadata were preserved without inference\. These components provide a harmonized resource for organizing, disseminating, and computationally analyzing peptide toxicity information\.The ontology\-guided organization of toxicity annotations is presented in Figure 2B\. The root category Toxic contains 57,080 available peptide\-endpoint states, including 13,824 positives, and comprises four primary classes, namely Cytotoxic \(25,454 available states; 7,122 positive\), Neurotoxic \(3,183; 1,481 positive\), Embryotoxic \(2 positive\), and Ichthyotoxic \(5 positive\)\. The Cytotoxic branch is further divided into Hemolytic \(35,960 available states; 4,714 positive\), Cytolysis \(343; 341 positive\), and Anti mammalian cells \(21,393 available states; 3,664 positive\), preserving more specific biological contexts\. These categories define the endpoint structure used throughout MAOMAO\.Evidence\-state distributions are summarized in Figure 2C and Supplementary Table S10\. Across MAOMAO, 31,153 states were positive, 91,506 negative, 15,717 ambiguous, and 5,044 unlabeled\. Because only positive annotations were propagated through the hierarchy, all other states remained endpoint\-specific, and no\-information states were excluded from the percentages shown in Figure 2C\. Toxic contained 13,824 positives, whereas Hemolytic had the highest proportion of ambiguous states \(19\.05%\) and was the only endpoint with unlabeled states, representing 14\.03% of its available annotations\.Across the seven non\-root endpoints, 7,331 of the 9,421 peptides with at least one positive annotation were assigned to multiple toxicity categories\. This corresponds to 77\.82% of positive peptides across these endpoints and 10\.2% of all MAOMAO sequences\. Percentages were calculated relative to the positive sequences assigned to each row endpoint and should therefore be interpreted directionally\. The largest overlap occurred between Cytotoxic and Hemolytic, with 4,128 shared sequences, representing 57\.96% of cytotoxic\-positive and 87\.57% of hemolytic\-positive sequences\. Complete pairwise counts and directional percentages are provided in Supplementary Section S2\.MAOMAO distributes harmonized annotations, numerical representations, benchmark resources, metadata, ontology definitions, and documentation across the functional layers shown in Figure 1B\.The Core Layer contains 574,856 harmonized peptide\-endpoint combinations corresponding to 71,857 unique sequences, together with ontology assignments, evidence classifications, provenance, and standardized metadata\. It additionally provides 169 HC50, LC50, LD50, and MHC measurement records\. Most were linked to the Core sequence universe, while six LD50 records remained unmatched because their sequences exceeded the 70\-residue limit\. One profile per Core sequence summarizes its activity annotations, supporting evidence, ontology effects, toxicity targets, selected descriptors, and available numerical toxicity properties\. The Descriptor Layer provides 41 features capturing sequence composition and physicochemical properties\.The Embedding Layer includes 10 protein\-language\-model embedding matrices and a one\-hot representation, all covering the complete set of 71,857 MAOMAO sequences\.The Benchmark Layer contains 300 endpoint\-seed\-strategy configurations generated through random and stratified five\-fold partitioning of five eligible endpoints \(Toxic, Cytotoxic, Hemolytic, Neurotoxic, and Anti mammalian cells\) using 30 random seeds\. These correspond to 1,500 data partitions and, across the 11 numerical representations, 3,300 representation\-specific configurations and 16,500 fold instances\. Associated parameters, reports, summaries, and execution records are also provided\.The Documentation Layer includes ontology definitions, metadata schemas, resource descriptions, versioning records, and licensing information\. Files are distributed in standard formats, including CSV, JSON, and YAML, with detailed component descriptions and inventories provided in Supplementary Sections S4\-S5\.To facilitate direct reuse of the distributed assets, MAOMAO provides five executable notebooks that operate on the released files rather than reconstructing the resource from the original sources\. The introductory workflow covers resource access, file validation, navigation of the Core Layer, and linkage of annotations, numerical representations, and benchmark partitions through stable sequence identifiers\. Complementary notebooks support descriptive characterization of endpoint states, class balance, co\-occurrence, sequence lengths, ontology consistency, and representation coverage, as well as retrieval and querying of individual sequence profiles\. Generated tables and figures are stored separately from the released resource files\.Two additional notebooks illustrate downstream machine\-learning reuse\. The neurotoxicity classification example joins a released train\-validation\-test partition with an existing protein language model representation and evaluates logistic regression, a linear support vector machine, and random forest models using fixed settings\. The quantitative regression example shows how MAOMAO&\#x27;s numerical toxicity measurements can be combined with a released sequence representation in a simple regression analysis\. These workflows are intended to demonstrate resource interoperability and reproducible reuse rather than establish state\-of\-the\-art predictors or replace the released benchmark design\. Detailed descriptions of the demonstration notebooks, execution requirements, and generated outputs are provided in Supplementary Section S6MAOMAO was designed as a reusable resource for peptide toxicity research, providing a harmonized collection of toxicity annotations, ontology mappings, evidence classifications, metadata records, numerical representations, and benchmark resources\.
